title: Building Canadian credit from scratch
summary: Lenders look at your Canadian credit history. Here is how it works and how to start building it early.
body:
Many newcomers arrive with a strong financial record from another country and find that it does not show up in Canada. Canadian lenders usually check your file at Canada's two main credit bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion. If you are new, that file may be thin or empty. This is common and it is fixable, but it takes time, so start early.

## How a credit file is built
Your file grows when you use credit and repay it on time: a credit card, a phone plan, a line of credit or a small loan. Payment history and how much of your available credit you use matter a great deal.

## Practical first steps
- Open a Canadian bank account and keep it in good standing.
- Get a credit card, even with a small limit, and pay the full balance on time every month.
- Keep your balances well below your limits.
- Check your credit report for free from both bureaus and correct any errors.

## Why it matters for buying a business
When you apply for an acquisition loan, the lender will look at your personal credit as well as the business. A short Canadian history does not stop you, but it can affect terms. Bring documents that show your financial track record elsewhere and ask each lender how they consider it.

title: Financing conversations as a newcomer
summary: How to prepare for conversations with Canadian lenders when your history is partly outside Canada.
body:
Lenders want to understand three things: the business, the buyer and the structure. As a newcomer, put extra care into the second.

## Prepare your story
- A clear résumé that translates your past roles into Canadian terms (see N3).
- Evidence of your savings and where they came from.
- Any financial records from your previous country, translated if needed.
- Your personal fit statement and thesis from Modules 0 and 1.

## Ask direct questions
- How do you consider credit history from outside Canada?
- How much equity would you expect from me?
- Does my immigration status affect eligibility for any of your products?

## Know what exists, and what it covers
BDC has a page for newcomer entrepreneurs with articles, a glossary in several languages and information on financing. Read it carefully: its newcomer financing information is written mainly for starting or growing a business, so ask BDC directly whether and how any newcomer product applies to **buying** an existing business. Do not assume it does.

## Keep options open
Speak with more than one lender. A bank, a credit union and BDC may see your situation differently.

title: Presenting your foreign experience, and Canadian business culture with owners
summary: Help sellers, brokers and lenders see the value of what you have done elsewhere, and build trust in a Canadian setting.
body:
Your experience abroad is an asset. The challenge is making it easy for Canadians to understand.

## Translate, don't just list
Describe what you did in terms a Canadian owner recognizes: the size of the team you managed, the revenue you were responsible for, the customers you served and the problems you solved. Replace local company names and titles with a short description. "Ran a 40-person regional distribution business with about $8 million in annual sales" is clearer than a title that does not exist here.

## Show the link to the business
Connect your experience to the business you want to buy. Your edge statement from Module 1 is the place to do it.

## Working with owners
Many sellers are long-time owners who care about their employees and community. In general, Canadian business conversations tend to value:
- Punctuality and follow-through on small promises
- A polite, fairly direct style without hard pressure
- Respect for what the owner built
- Written confirmation of what was agreed

Customs vary by region, industry and person, so watch and adapt. In Québec, using French is usually a sign of respect and often a practical requirement (see N4).

## References
If you can, ask former colleagues or clients to act as references, and be ready to explain how to contact them.

title: Québec and French terms
summary: If you plan to buy in Québec, French is the language of business. Here are key terms and where to learn more.
body:
Québec has its own language law, and French is the normal language of work and commerce there. If you buy a business in Québec, plan to run it in French: with employees, in signage, in many documents and with many customers. Ask your lawyer which rules apply to the business you are buying.

## Useful terms
- **Repreneuriat**: taking over an existing business (business transfer from the buyer's side)
- **Repreneur / repreneuse**: the buyer who takes over a business
- **Cédant / cédante**: the owner who transfers the business
- **Relève**: succession, the next generation of owners
- **Lettre d'intention**: letter of intent
- **Vérification diligente**: due diligence
- **Convention d'achat**: purchase agreement
- **Achat d'actions / achat d'actifs**: share purchase / asset purchase
- **Solde de prix de vente (balance de prix de vente)**: vendor take-back / seller note
- **Fonds de roulement**: working capital
- **BAIIA**: EBITDA

## Where to go
Repreneuriat Québec supports buyers and sellers throughout the province. The Office québécois de la langue française publishes terminology resources.

title: Immigration status and business ownership
summary: General information only. Your status can affect what you may do in Canada, so get advice from a licensed professional before you commit.
body:
This page is general information, not immigration advice. Immigration rules change and depend on your situation. Before you sign anything, speak with a licensed immigration lawyer or a licensed immigration consultant.

## Why status matters
Your immigration status can affect whether you may work in Canada, in what role and for how long. Owning shares in a company is different from working in it, and the rules can treat them differently. Some programs link business ownership to immigration, at the federal level and in some provinces, including a Québec entrepreneur stream focused on taking over a business. Each has its own conditions.

## Questions to take to a licensed professional
- Can I own this business with my current status?
- Can I work in the business, and in what role?
- Would buying this business affect any application I have or plan to make?
- Are there timing issues I need to plan around?

## Choose a licensed professional
Lawyers are licensed by provincial and territorial law societies. Immigration consultants must be licensed by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants. Check a licence before paying anyone.

Owning a business does not, on its own, give you immigration status. Make your purchase decision on business grounds, with immigration advice as a separate check.

title: Extra people for your Deal Team
summary: Settlement agencies and newcomer-business programs can widen your network and support you through the search.
body:
Your core Deal Team is the same as for any buyer. Newcomers can add people who understand the extra steps.

## Who to add
- **A settlement agency.** Government-funded services can help with language training, credential recognition and local connections. Many are free for eligible newcomers.
- **A newcomer-business program.** Many cities have entrepreneurship programs for newcomers, with workshops, mentoring and introductions.
- **A licensed immigration professional,** if your status affects your plans (see N5).
- **A mentor from your community** who has owned a Canadian business.
- **An interpreter or translator** for documents, if you need one. Your lawyer can tell you when certified translation is required.

## How to use them
Add them to your private Deal Team list on NextOwner with their role and status, so you can see your whole support network in one place.
